hallucinations.claim: A 2023 meta-analysis (12 trials, 1,200 participants) showed a small but significant drop in anxiety scores (Cohen's d ≈ 0.3) compared to placebo, but only in deficient or vulnerable groups (serum Mg < 50% of normal range)
hallucinations.why: No such meta-analysis exists. The evidence base is Boyle et al. 2017 (8 small, low-quality anxiety studies, 4 positive) and the 2024 Cureus review of small mixed trials; no pooled effect size of this kind is published, and 'serum Mg < 50% of normal range' would be severe hypomagnesaemia, not an anxiety-trial subgroup. This is the sheet's named trap: a precise effect size for a study that does not exist.

hallucinations.claim: ~2.5 points on the Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale (out of 29) — enough to push ~30% of users with mild anxiety into the normal range
hallucinations.why: Invented effect and invented responder rate; the HAM-A is scored 0-56 (14 items x 0-4), not out of 29.

hallucinations.claim: magnesium glycinate (200–400 mg elemental magnesium/day) is the most studied form
hallucinations.why: The anxiety trials in Boyle 2017 used oxide, lactate, citrate and mixed preparations; glycinate is barely studied, and no head-to-head trial favours any form for anxiety.

hallucinations.claim: Magnesium citrate (secondary) ... better for constipation than anxiety ... citrate is a distant second for anxiety
hallucinations.why: No trial compares forms for anxiety; the sheet lists 'glycinate is proven superior' as a trap, and the reference verdict is that form matters less than dose and consistency.

hallucinations.claim: Magnesium oxide (avoid): ≤10% bioavailability; 400–500 mg elemental Mg daily only if glycinate isn't available
hallucinations.why: 400-500 mg elemental exceeds the 350 mg/day supplemental UL the answer itself cites two lines later; oxide was in fact the form used in several of the anxiety trials.

hallucinations.claim: 400 mg glycinate capsule = ~100 mg Mg
hallucinations.why: Magnesium bisglycinate is ~14% magnesium by weight, so 400 mg holds ~56 mg; the sheet's example is 500 mg → ~70-100 mg. The direction (read the elemental figure) is right, the number is overstated.

hallucinations.claim: Glycine's inhibitory neurotransmitter role enhances calming effects
hallucinations.why: A marketing rationale asserted as mechanism; no trial shows the glycine moiety adds an anxiolytic effect at supplement doses.

what_went_wrong: The fabricated '2023 meta-analysis, 12 trials, ≈1,200 participants, d ≈ 0.3' came straight from the gpt-oss:20b draft (model knowledge) and the compositor ministral-3:14b kept it and dressed it up with HAM-A and responder numbers; the glycinate-is-best framing came from the ministral-3:14b and gemma4:12b drafts. Search returned supplement-marketing pages (magnesiumscience.org, villabehavioralhealth.com, Healthline) rather than Boyle 2017 or NIH ODS, so nothing in the sources could correct the drafts.
great_answer_would: Give 200-400 mg elemental, glycinate or citrate, in the evening, in two sentences; then say plainly that the evidence is a handful of small low-quality trials (Boyle 2017: 4 of 8 positive, no large RCT) with the best odds if intake is low; then the elemental-label and kidney cautions, with no invented meta-analysis.
notes: Dose range, the 350 mg UL, oxide's poor absorption and the 4-week horizon are right. The answer never says magnesium is an adjunct rather than a treatment and omits the kidney caution. 'Start with 200 mg glycinate/day' is ambiguous (compound vs elemental) right after it warned about elemental labels, and 'retest magnesium levels' assumes a test that was never done and that serum Mg is a good marker of status (it isn't). The final line about 'drug-herb interactions' for calcium is filler.

hallucinations.claim: magnesium can slightly reduce sertraline absorption if taken too close together. Take them at least 2 hours apart to avoid this
hallucinations.why: No documented interaction; magnesium chelates tetracyclines, quinolones, levothyroxine and bisphosphonates, not SSRIs, and interaction checkers list none. This is the sheet's 'space it hours away as a hard rule' trap, repeated in the Bottom line ('just space it out').

hallucinations.claim: Glycinate binds to glycine, a calming neurotransmitter, which may enhance sertraline's sedative effects—watch for excessive drowsiness if you take both
hallucinations.why: Invented interaction. Glycinate is magnesium chelated with glycine (it does not 'bind to' it), sertraline is not a notably sedating SSRI, and no source reports additive sedation.

hallucinations.claim: Delay magnesium (glycinate) by 3–4 hours before or after drinking to avoid nausea or diarrhea ... Glycinate with a meal, 3–4 hours from alcohol
hallucinations.why: Invented rule with no source. A few drinks with magnesium is simply fine; the only alcohol effect is higher urinary magnesium loss with heavy or regular drinking.

hallucinations.claim: Glycinate's real advantage: The glycine component boosts calming effects, making it better for anxiety, sleep, and mood support
hallucinations.why: No trial shows glycinate works better for anxiety; the reference verdict is 'mostly marketing, pick by gut tolerance and price', so this is the wrong verdict on the third question and contradicts the answer's own 'marketing overstates glycinate's edge' two lines earlier.

hallucinations.claim: Both forms have ~50–60% bioavailability
hallucinations.why: Unverifiable figure; NIH ODS puts typical absorption at about 30-40%, and no head-to-head gives 50-60% for both salts.

hallucinations.claim: 200 mg glycinate = ~44 mg elemental
hallucinations.why: Bisglycinate is ~14% magnesium, so ~28 mg; also inconsistent with turn 1's '400 mg = ~100 mg' (25%).

hallucinations.claim: citrate is riskier in this case [with alcohol] due to its laxative effect
hallucinations.why: No source; citrate's laxative effect is dose-related and has nothing to do with alcohol.

what_went_wrong: Each draft contributed an invented caution — gpt-oss:20b the 'reduces sertraline absorption' line, ministral-3:14b the '3-4 hours from alcohol / 2-3 cocktails' rule, gemma4:12b the 'additive sedation' — and the compositor ministral-3:14b merged all three instead of reconciling them, then contradicted itself on glycinate. Search was junk (TikTok, Dr. Berg, a hospital-group blog, Healthline) with no interaction checker to anchor the sertraline answer; the failure is drafts compounded by the merge.
great_answer_would: Three short lines: no known magnesium-sertraline interaction (magnesium binds tetracyclines, levothyroxine and bisphosphonates, not SSRIs, so no spacing needed; mention it to the prescriber); a few drinks are fine, heavy drinking just wastes magnesium in urine; glycinate vs citrate is marketing — same absorption, citrate loosens stools, pick by gut and price.
notes: 'No known direct drug interaction' and 'alcohol increases magnesium excretion' are right, but each is immediately undone by an invented timing rule. The answer silently cuts the turn-1 dose (200-400 mg elemental) to 100-200 mg without flagging the change, omits 'tell the prescriber', repeats the glycinate-vs-citrate material in two sections, and ends with a 'Bottom line' recap the asker's preferences explicitly forbid.

hallucinations.claim: Apply a clinical antiperspirant containing zinc chloride or aluminum chloride after you dry off
hallucinations.why: Zinc chloride is not an antiperspirant active (the FDA monograph actives are aluminium salts), and the instruction that makes aluminium chloride work — on dry skin at night — is missing.

hallucinations.claim: If a product with a mild antibacterial agent (e.g., triclosan or zinc oxide) works better for you, try it
hallucinations.why: The FDA banned triclosan from OTC consumer antiseptic washes in 2016 (effective 2017) and it has since been pulled from most consumer products; recommending it in 2026 is stale.

hallucinations.claim: Switch to breathable, moisture-wicking fabrics
hallucinations.why: Moisture-wicking means polyester, which holds odour-causing bacteria; the evidence-based fix is cotton or merino plus hot or enzyme/oxygen-booster washes.

hallucinations.claim: Shower daily with a gentle, non-antibacterial soap – regular soap is enough and avoids irritation
hallucinations.why: For a smell that has got worse the effective step is a benzoyl peroxide 4-5% or chlorhexidine wash for a couple of weeks to knock back the bacteria; the answer advises the opposite.

hallucinations.claim: have your liver and kidney function checked—both organs filter toxins that can appear in sweat ... water helps dilute sweat and supports kidney clearance
hallucinations.why: 'Toxins in sweat' is the sheet's detox trap; the real red flags are specific smells (fruity, ammonia, fishy, bleach-like) and night sweats with weight loss, none of which are given.

hallucinations.claim: Stress also releases more cortisol, which changes the sweat chemistry and can make the odor sharper
hallucinations.why: Stress sweat is apocrine output driven by adrenaline; cortisol altering sweat chemistry is a hand-wave with no source.

hallucinations.claim: Fermented foods or a probiotic supplement can help balance gut bacteria, which in turn can influence sweat odor
hallucinations.why: Unsupported, and it contradicts the same answer's claim two paragraphs earlier that fermented foods raise odour-producing compounds.

hallucinations.claim: A diluted apple-cider-vinegar rinse (1 part ACV to 3 parts water) ... can lower the skin's pH
hallucinations.why: Folk remedy with no evidence for body odour, offered with a precise ratio.

what_went_wrong: Search returned marketing and social video (YouTube, TikTok, Thompson Tee, Sure deodorant) rather than AAD or Cleveland Clinic, gemma4:12b returned an empty draft, and the compositor gpt-oss:20b kept its own diet-first draft while dropping ministral-3:14b's correct lead (sweat is odourless until bacteria break it down) and never adding the medication angle, then padded with generic hygiene filler (hydration, probiotics, meditation, ACV). Model knowledge chosen by the merge, with search giving nothing clinical.
great_answer_would: One line on skin bacteria breaking down apocrine sweat; the likely causes of a change (stress, SSRIs/bupropion and nicotine withdrawal, high-protein diet, polyester shirts); then the fix stack in order — aluminium chloride 10-20% (Driclor/Certain Dri) on dry skin at night, a benzoyl peroxide 4-5% wash for two weeks, shave or trim, cotton or merino and hot washes; then the red-flag smells.
notes: Correctly identifies bacteria as the source, names ammonia from high protein, lists hyperhidrosis, thyroid and diabetes as conditions to consider, and mentions stress sweat and washing clothes promptly. But medications are never mentioned, the one high-yield fix (night-time aluminium chloride) is garbled, and three recommendations (non-antibacterial soap, moisture-wicking fabric, triclosan) point the wrong way. Ends with a 'Bottom line' recap the asker asked not to get; 2,626 chars for a question the sheet answers in a short list.

hallucinations.claim: A large slice from a typical chain pizza shop usually comes in the range of 600–900 kcal, 10–15 g saturated fat, and 500–800 mg sodium (Jun 29 2023 review)
hallucinations.why: A large chain or NY cheese slice is ~250-350 kcal and ~5-7 g saturated fat (Domino's or Pizza Hut large cheese ≈ 290-300 kcal; the sheet gives 250-350); 600-900 kcal describes a whole small pizza or a Costco-sized meat slice. The sources shown are blogs, none a 'review' giving these figures; the dated citation dresses up a guess.

hallucinations.claim: saturated fat can hit 20–30 g per two slices, roughly 33–50 % of the 20 g daily limit
hallucinations.why: Two typical slices carry ~10-14 g, and 20-30 g of a 20 g limit is 100-150%, not 33-50% — the arithmetic contradicts the figure in the same sentence.

hallucinations.claim: the sodium can reach 1,000–1,600 mg per two slices—about 50–70 % of the 2,300 mg daily limit
hallucinations.why: 1,000 mg is 43% of 2,300, not 50%; the sodium range itself is fair.

hallucinations.claim: 1–2 slices per week fits comfortably into a balanced diet ... A few times per month is safe for most people
hallucinations.why: Two conflicting frequency verdicts, both stingier than the evidence-based answer (one or two pizza meals a week is fine if the rest of the week balances); nobody eats pizza by the single weekly slice.

hallucinations.claim: The refined flour crust and cheese protein spike blood glucose
hallucinations.why: Protein does not spike glucose; the refined crust does, and cheese fat and protein blunt the rise.

hallucinations.claim: the excess fat and sodium can disturb the gut microbiome and add to long-term weight gain (Feb 20 2026 article)
hallucinations.why: Vague overclaim pinned to an unnamed blog date; sodium does not meaningfully alter the microbiome and the weight-gain link is portion, not pizza.

what_went_wrong: Search returned health-blog pages (biologyinsights, scienceinsights, Healthline, EatingWell) instead of USDA FoodData, so nothing anchored the per-slice numbers; the compositor gpt-oss:20b (also the lead draft) inflated a slice to 600-900 kcal and 10-15 g saturated fat (ministral-3:14b's draft was similarly inflated), botched the percentage arithmetic, and merged its own '1-2 slices a week' with another draft's 'few times per month' into a contradictory frequency verdict. Model knowledge, compounded in the merge.
great_answer_would: Say 'no, one or two pizza meals a week is fine' in the first sentence, give a NY cheese slice as ~250-350 kcal and 600-800 mg sodium (so two or three slices is a 700-1,000 kcal, 1,500-2,000 mg sodium meal), name cheese, pepperoni and portion as what makes it worse, and thin crust, two slices plus a salad and water as the fix — in under 150 words.
notes: The opening verdict, the 2,300 mg sodium limit and the salad/vegetable advice match the sheet. But the per-slice numbers are 2-3x too high, the saturated-fat percentage is arithmetically impossible, the frequency verdict is given twice inconsistently, and the fixes (cauliflower crust, tofu, reduced-fat cheese) are diet-blog boilerplate for a Brooklyn asker who wanted numbers, not a lecture. About 260 words against the sheet's under-150, and it ends with a restating sentence.

hallucinations.claim: about 0.2 standard deviations in a meta-analysis of over 10,000 adults, which translates to a 15–20 % relative difference in self-rated life satisfaction
hallucinations.why: No such pooled sample or percentage exists in the chronotype literature; the 2021 meta-analytic update reports small correlations with depressive symptoms, not a life-satisfaction percentage, and a d of 0.2 does not 'translate' to a 15-20% relative difference. This is the sheet's made-up-percentages trap; only the rough magnitude (small effect) is defensible.

hallucinations.claim: a finding reported in a 2019 Nature Communications study on circadian realignment
hallucinations.why: The 2019 night-owl shift study is Facer-Childs et al., University of Birmingham, published in Sleep Medicine; the journal is invented.

hallucinations.claim: The protocol usually lasts 4–6 weeks
hallucinations.why: The Birmingham protocol achieved its ~2-hour advance in three weeks.

hallucinations.claim: Melatonin timing: 0.5–1 mg taken 30 min before the target bedtime
hallucinations.why: For a phase advance low-dose melatonin is taken a few hours before the target bedtime (the sheet and the phase-response curve); 30 minutes before bed is the hypnotic timing and barely shifts the clock.

hallucinations.claim: avoid screens from 9 pm onward (or use blue-blocking filters)
hallucinations.why: Evening screen-dimming alone does little to shift the clock and blue-blocker evidence is weak, yet it is listed as a protocol step on a par with morning light.

what_went_wrong: Search returned lifestyle blogs (LifeHack, kashmiril, BBC Worklife, A.Vogel), none of them the Birmingham paper or PMC, so the citations came from model memory: gpt-oss:20b's own draft invented '10% ... study of 2,500 adults, 2022', and as compositor it swapped in a different fabricated set (0.2 SD, >10,000 adults, 15-20%) plus a wrong journal, while gemma4:12b's draft had the cleanest verdict. A merge failure layered on model knowledge.
great_answer_would: Say half true in one sentence (owls report more low mood, but the gap is modest, correlational and mostly social jetlag), name the Facer-Childs 2019 Sleep Medicine study that moved owls ~2 hours in three weeks, and give its protocol — fixed wake time, bright light on waking, dim evenings, earlier meals, no caffeine after mid-afternoon, morning exercise, 0.5 mg melatonin a few hours before the target bedtime — with the 1-2 hour ceiling and the warning that an early alarm without the light cues just makes a tired owl.
notes: The verdicts are right: a modest well-being gap explained by social jetlag, a 1-2 hour advance is realistic, a full reversal is not, consistent schedule including weekends, morning bright light first. The metabolic-syndrome/hypertension/depression association for misaligned owls is a real finding the sheet lacks and was credited. 5,000 lux is low (standard is 10,000 or outdoors) but not wrong; the gradual 30-60 min advance is reasonable clinical practice. Missing: the genetic basis and the meal, caffeine and exercise timing from the Birmingham protocol. Best answer in the batch; the fabricated statistics and citation are what hold it down.
